metadata.disclaimer: This FAQ is compiled from experiences shared by caregivers and patients in the ALS Care & Support India community representing 10+ years of collective wisdom from 650+ families. It is intended for educational purposes only and does NOT constitute medical advice. Every ALS patient's condition is unique. Always consult your neurologist, pulmonologist, or treating physician before making any medical decisions.

categories.name: Getting Started with ALS Care
categories.description: First steps after diagnosis, building care teams, and understanding the basics

questions.question: My loved one was just diagnosed with ALS. We are completely lost. Where do we even start?
questions.answer:
**Take a deep breath.** Many families in our community were in the same place. Here's what helped them get organized:

**Week 1 Priorities:**

1. **Join a support community** - Introduce yourself, mention your city, current symptoms, and stage. The community will guide based on your specific situation.

2. **Get baseline assessments done:**
   • FVC (lung function test) - critical for respiratory planning
   • Swallowing assessment
   • Overall strength evaluation

3. **Start researching equipment NOW** - Even if you don't need it today. When you need a BiPAP at 2 AM urgently, you don't want to be searching for vendors.

4. **Involve your PALS in all decisions** - Many patients feel they've lost control. Keeping them involved helps emotionally.

5. **Don't Google too much initially** - It will scare you with worst-case scenarios. Real families have PALS living 5, 8, even 10+ years with good care.
questions.recommendation: Focus on quality of life, not statistics. Every patient is different.

questions.question: What do PALS and CALS mean?
questions.answer:
These are terms commonly used in the ALS community worldwide:

**PALS** = Person/Patient with ALS (the patient themselves)
**CALS** = Caregiver of person with ALS (family members, hired help)

We use these terms because they're shorter to type and also remind us that the patient is a PERSON first, not just a 'patient' or 'case'.

questions.question: How do I know what stage my PALS is at?
questions.answer:
Here's how we typically think about stages based on practical care needs:

**Early Stage:**
• Can walk (maybe with support)
• Can eat normally or with minor difficulty
• Can breathe on own, SpO₂ stays above 95%
• Needs help with some activities but mostly independent

**Middle Stage:**
• Wheelchair dependent or very limited walking
• Eating takes longer (30-45+ minutes), some choking
• May need BiPAP at night, SpO₂ drops sometimes
• Speech becoming unclear

**Advanced Stage:**
• Bed-bound or fully wheelchair dependent
• On feeding tube (PEG/Ryles)
• BiPAP most of the day or on tracheostomy
• Needs 24/7 care for everything

**Important:** Staging is less important than watching for specific warning signs that tell you when to act.

categories.name: Breathing Support & BiPAP
categories.description: Critical respiratory support, BiPAP usage, ventilator settings, and when to act

questions.question: When does a PALS need BiPAP support and what are the signs?
questions.answer:
**Key Understanding:** In ALS, the problem is NOT oxygen getting in, but CO₂ (carbon dioxide) getting OUT. When breathing muscles weaken, CO₂ builds up in the blood. Plain oxygen can mask this problem - SpO₂ may look normal while CO₂ reaches dangerous levels.

**BiPAP works differently:** It pushes air in (helps oxygen) AND helps push CO₂ out by supporting the breathing muscles.

**DEFINITE SIGNS (act immediately):**
• Cannot lie flat - needs 2-3 pillows or sleeps in recliner (orthopnea)
• Waking up with headaches (CO₂ building up at night)
• SpO₂ dropping below 94% at any time
• Feeling breathless at rest or while talking

**EARLY WARNING SIGNS (start planning):**
• More tired than usual, sleeping more during day
• Morning grogginess that doesn't go away
• Difficulty completing long sentences without pausing
• Yawning frequently (body trying to get more oxygen)
• Weak cough - can't clear throat properly

**Oxygen Only vs BiPAP:**
| Aspect | Oxygen Only | BiPAP |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| Increases O₂ | Yes | Yes |
| Removes CO₂ | NO | YES |
| Supports breathing muscles | NO | YES |
| Safe for ALS alone | RISKY | RECOMMENDED |
questions.warning: Several families delayed BiPAP and ended up with emergency tracheostomies. Those who started early are often still on BiPAP years later with good quality of life.
questions.recommendation: If you see these signs, consult your pulmonologist about starting BiPAP early. Don't wait!

questions.question: Doctor said SpO2 is 96% so no BiPAP needed. But he can't sleep flat and gets breathless. Should we wait?
questions.answer:
**NO, don't wait!** This is a common mistake.

**Why these signs matter:**
• Can't sleep flat (orthopnea) = earliest sign of diaphragm weakness
• Breathlessness with activity = respiratory muscles struggling

**The Hidden Problem:** Daytime SpO₂ may be fine, but it drops significantly at night when diaphragm works harder. Many PALS have normal daytime readings but drop to 85-88% during sleep.

**What to do:**
1. Get overnight pulse oximetry or sleep study
2. If SpO₂ drops below 93-94% at night, push for BiPAP
3. Buy a good pulse oximeter (₹1,500-3,000) for home monitoring

if_then.then: Immediate BiPAP evaluation needed - don't delay

if_then.if: Only slight fatigue with normal SpO₂
if_then.then: Discuss with pulmonologist - may not be urgent yet but start preparing

questions.warning: SpO₂ of 96% during day means nothing - it drops at night. Many PALS have normal daytime SpO₂ but drop to 85-88% at night.

questions.question: Which BiPAP machine should I buy? What are the options and costs in India?
questions.answer:
**For ALS patients, machines with volume-assured modes (AVAPS/iVAPS) are recommended** because they adapt as the disease progresses.

**Recommended Machines:**

| Machine | Approx. Cost | Notes |
|---------|--------------|-------|
| ResMed Stellar 150 | ₹3.0 lakhs | iVAPS mode, works with tracheostomy, built-in battery. Most popular in community. |
| Philips Trilogy 100 | ₹4.5 lakhs | Versatile, portable, AVAPS-AE mode. Excellent for invasive/non-invasive. |
| Philips DreamStation AVAPS | ₹1.0 lakh | Good budget option with AVAPS mode. May need Whisper Swivel for tracheostomy. |
| ResMed Lumis 150 | ₹1.5-1.8 lakhs | Same iVAPS mode as Stellar, slightly fewer features. Good budget option. |

if_then.if: Planning for long-term home care with possible tracheostomy
if_then.then: Consider Stellar 150 or Trilogy 100 from the start
Start with DreamStation AVAPS, plan upgrade later

questions.recommendation: Buy from authorized dealers only. Get proper training. MOST IMPORTANTLY - buy a second backup machine (can be used/refurbished for ₹60-80k). When your main machine fails at 3 AM, you'll thank yourself.

questions.question: What's the difference between S/T mode, AVAPS, and iVAPS?
questions.answer:
**S/T MODE (Spontaneous/Timed):**
• You set a fixed pressure (e.g., IPAP 14, EPAP 6)
• Machine gives same pressure for every breath
• Problem: As ALS progresses and muscles weaken, fixed pressure may not be enough
• You have to keep manually increasing settings

**AVAPS MODE (Philips machines):**
• You set a TARGET volume (e.g., 400ml per breath)
• Machine automatically adjusts pressure to achieve this target
• Much better for ALS because it adapts to changing needs

**iVAPS MODE (ResMed machines):**
• Same concept as AVAPS
• Has extra smart features like learning patient's breathing pattern

**Best Analogy:** S/T is like setting AC to blow at fixed speed. AVAPS/iVAPS is like setting AC to maintain room at 24°C - it adjusts automatically to achieve the goal.
questions.recommendation: AVAPS or iVAPS is much better for ALS because the machine adapts as disease progresses.

questions.question: What BiPAP settings should we start with?
questions.answer:
**Recommended starting settings for iVAPS/AVAPS mode** (always confirm with your pulmonologist):

• **Mode:** iVAPS or AVAPS
• **Height:** Enter patient's height (machine calculates target volume from this)
• **Tidal Volume:** Approximately 7 × weight in kg (e.g., 60 kg patient = ~420ml)
• **EPAP:** 5-6 cm H₂O
• **PS Min/IPAP Min:** 4 cm H₂O
• **PS Max/IPAP Max:** 12-14 cm H₂O (can increase later if needed)
• **Target Rate/BPM:** 15 breaths/minute
• **Rise Time:** 200-300ms (increase to 300ms if pressure rise feels too fast)

if_then.then: Check mask fit, circuit connections, or cuff inflation
Gradually increase IPAP Max by 1-2 cm H₂O

questions.recommendation: For first few days, use during daytime while watching TV to get used to it. Don't start at night - it's harder to adapt when you're trying to sleep.

questions.question: Should we use oxygen concentrator with BiPAP?
questions.answer:
**Critical Warning:** Plain oxygen ALONE should NEVER be used for ALS patients!

**Why It's Dangerous:** In ALS, the problem is weak breathing muscles, not lack of oxygen. Plain oxygen:
• Masks the real problem
• Causes CO₂ retention (can be fatal)
• Reduces body's natural drive to breathe

**When O₂ CAN Be Used:**
• ONLY with BiPAP, never alone
• During infections when SpO₂ remains low despite BiPAP
• As advised by pulmonologist

**How to Connect:** Use oxygen enrichment port on ventilator/BiPAP - NOT directly to patient. Flow rate: Typically 1-2 LPM.

if_then.then: First check secretions, settings, circuit. Only add O₂ if still needed.
Always use WITH BiPAP, never alone for ALS patients

categories.name: Tracheostomy Care
categories.description: When to consider tracheostomy, daily care, suctioning, and managing complications

questions.question: Doctor is recommending tracheostomy. How do we decide if it's time?
questions.answer:
**Signs that it may be time:**
• BiPAP 20+ hours daily and still having SpO₂ drops
• Frequent desaturation even with BiPAP optimized
• Secretions that can't be managed with oral/nasal suction
• Repeated chest infections/aspiration
• CO₂ levels staying high (check ABG)

**Important considerations:**

1. **PLANNED vs EMERGENCY:** Planned tracheostomy with time to prepare is SO much better than emergency tracheostomy during a crisis.

2. **QUALITY OF LIFE:** Many PALS on trach have BETTER quality of life - no mask on face, can eat more easily (sometimes), more stable breathing.

3. **PATIENT'S CHOICE:** Most importantly - what does your PALS want? This should be THEIR decision.

4. **CARE REQUIREMENTS:** Trach requires regular suctioning, tube changes, 24/7 trained caregiver. Ensure this can be arranged before proceeding.
perspectives: We were terrified of tracheostomy. But after 2 emergency admissions in one month, we did planned trach. It's been 2 years now. My husband is stable. I wish we'd done it sooner.
My mother chose not to have tracheostomy. We respected her decision. She passed peacefully at home. There's no wrong answer.
questions.warning: Whatever you decide, do NOT let it become an emergency decision. If leaning towards trach, plan it. If declining trach, ensure palliative care is in place.

questions.question: How do I suction properly without hurting my PALS?
questions.answer:
**Training comes first:** Suction technique, catheter size, depth, pressure and equipment differ by person and airway. Arrange practical instruction and a written plan with a respiratory therapist, trained ICU nurse or doctor; an online sequence is not enough.

**Before and during suction:** Use the prescribed equipment and hygiene technique. Suction only when indicated and as taught. Routine saline instillation into the tracheostomy is generally avoided; do not use force or keep repeating ineffective attempts.

**Stop and escalate:** If the suction catheter will not pass, the TT tube may be blocked or displaced. Call 112 and the respiratory/ICU team now. Do not force the catheter, squeeze an Ambu bag harder, or attempt ventilation through a tube whose patency and position are uncertain. If external checks and any prescribed, trained suction do not promptly restore effective breathing, stop repeated attempts and obtain urgent skilled help. If the person worsens, escalate immediately. Do not delay help for nebulization or repeated suction cycles.

**If suction causes bleeding or worsening distress:** Stop and seek clinical advice; severe distress, significant bleeding or ineffective ventilation needs immediate emergency help. Do not assume that blood is just minor suction trauma.

TT removal/replacement and cuff interventions require a doctor, respiratory therapist or ICU nurse competent and authorized in emergency tracheostomy care. A ventilator technician can help with equipment, but must have specific clinical training and authorization to perform airway procedures. A caregiver should perform an airway intervention only if specifically trained and authorized in that person’s written emergency plan.

[Emergency guidance and sources](/emergency-protocol).

categories.name: Feeding & Nutrition
categories.description: PEG tube placement, feeding protocols, managing blockages, and nutritional guidance

questions.question: My PALS is taking 1.5 hours to finish one meal and coughing throughout. Should we consider a feeding tube?
questions.answer:
**This is a situation many families face.** Here's what has worked for others:

**UNDERSTAND THEIR FEAR:**
• They see it as 'giving up'
• Fear of surgery (for PEG)
• Loss of pleasure of eating

**HOW TO APPROACH THE CONVERSATION:**

1. **Reframe the purpose:** It's not about STOPPING oral eating. It's about getting nutrition without exhaustion. They can STILL taste food if they want - small amounts for pleasure.

2. **Address specific fears:** PEG surgery is minor - 15-20 minute procedure. Tube is hidden under clothes.

3. **Involve them in decisions:** Let them choose when, which hospital, etc.

**RISK OF WAITING:**
• 1.5 hours for a meal = extreme exhaustion
• Coughing = aspiration risk = pneumonia
• Each pneumonia episode weakens further
• Emergency tube insertion is harder than planned
questions.warning: If meals taking 1+ hours with frequent choking, the risk of aspiration pneumonia is significant. Don't delay too long.

questions.question: What's better - PEG tube or Ryles (NG) tube?
questions.answer:
**PEG is MUCH better for long-term use.** Here's why:

| Aspect | Ryles (NG) Tube | PEG Tube |
|--------|-----------------|----------|
| Location | Through nose into stomach | Through abdomen into stomach |
| Visibility | Visible on face | Hidden under clothes |
| Comfort | Can irritate nose/throat | Much more comfortable |
| Duration | Change every 2-3 months | Lasts 6-12 months |
| BiPAP compatibility | Creates leak with mask | No interference |
| Cost | ₹500-2,000 | ₹15,000-40,000 |
questions.recommendation: If tube feeding needed for more than a few weeks, go straight to PEG. Don't waste time with Ryles.

questions.question: PEG tube got blocked completely. What do I do?
questions.answer:
**Don't panic!** Try these in order:

1. **WARM WATER FLUSH:** Fill 50ml syringe with warm (not hot) water. Push gently.

2. **THE COLA TRICK:** Yes, seriously! Clamp the tube, fill with Coca-Cola or similar carbonated drink, leave for 30-60 minutes, then try flushing with water. The acid and fizz break down the blockage.

3. **ENZYME SOLUTION:** Ask pharmacist for pancreatic enzyme powder. Mix with water, inject into tube, wait 30 min, flush.

4. **MECHANICAL CLEANING:** Get PEG tube cleaning brush from Amazon (₹99). Gently insert and rotate.

**HOW TO PREVENT BLOCKAGES:**
• Flush 30-50ml water BEFORE every feed
• Flush 70-100ml water AFTER every feed (most important!)
• Don't give very thick feeds - thin them down
• Crush medications very finely, use liquid medications when possible

questions.question: How much and how often should we feed through PEG?
questions.answer:
**General Guidelines:**
• Feed per meal: 150-250ml
• Total daily: 1500-2000ml across 6-8 feeds
• Feed duration: Slow over 15-20 minutes (not bolus)

**Sample Schedule:** 7am, 10am, 1pm, 4pm, 7pm, 10pm

**Critical Steps:**
• Flush with 30ml water BEFORE feeding
• Flush with 50-70ml water AFTER feeding
• Keep bed elevated 30-45° during and 30-40 minutes after

**Feed Consistency:** Smooth, no lumps. Use high-speed blender.

**Protein Needs:** 1-1.5g per kg body weight daily. Add whey protein isolate if needed.

if_then.then: Reduce quantity per feed, increase frequency, check for acid reflux
Add more fiber, ensure adequate water, consider laxatives

categories.name: Essential Equipment Guide
categories.description: Essential equipment, power backup, and home ICU setup guidance with India-specific costs

questions.question: What basic monitoring and respiratory equipment do I need?
questions.answer:
**MONITORING (Essential):**

• **Pulse Oximeter** - ₹1,500-3,000
  Measures SpO₂ and pulse. Normal SpO₂: 95-99%. Below 90% needs intervention.

• **Ambu Bag** - ₹2,000 (MUST HAVE 2-3)
  Manual resuscitation for emergencies. Use when BiPAP fails or during power outages.

**RESPIRATORY:**

• **Suction Machine** - ₹6,000-8,000 (Yuwell recommended)
  Essential for tracheostomy, useful even before. Set pressure to 100-120 mmHg.

• **Nebulizer Machine** - ₹1,500-3,000
  Delivers medication to lungs. Common: Duolin, Budecort, NS, Mucinac.

• **Cough Assist Machine** - ~₹2 lakhs
  Helps clear phlegm. Models: T70 (basic) vs E70 (advanced).
questions.warning: Have BACKUP equipment for BiPAP, suction, and nebulizer. Equipment failure during emergency can be life-threatening.

questions.question: What power backup do I need for BiPAP and other equipment?
questions.answer:
**Power backup is CRITICAL. Without it, a power cut can be life-threatening.**

**HOME BACKUP:**
• Standard home inverter (e.g., Luminous) with adequate battery
• Calculate: BiPAP uses 50-100W, suction ~100W, nebulizer ~50W
• Ensure inverter can handle total load + buffer

**Equipment Backup Costs:**
| Equipment | Cost | Purpose |
|-----------|------|----------|
| Home Inverter (2KVA min) | ₹15,000-30,000 | 4-6 hours backup |
| Generator (2-3 KVA) | ₹25,000-50,000 | Extended outages |
| Portable Battery Pack | ₹15,000-25,000 | Short outages/travel |
| Ambu Bag | ₹2,000 | Manual backup - no power needed |
| Oxygen Cylinder | ₹5,000-8,000 | Concentrator needs power |
questions.recommendation: Apply for essential/medical connection from electricity board. Medical connections get priority restoration.

categories.name: Emergency Protocols
categories.description: These notes draw on personal caregiving experience and shared family learning. They are not a clinician-validated emergency protocol or a substitute for the person’s written, individualized emergency plan and hands-on training with the treating team. Call 112 immediately in India for severe or worsening breathing difficulty, ineffective ventilation, suspected blocked or displaced tracheostomy, blue/grey colour, collapse or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for a particular SpO2 reading or try every step first.

questions.question: SpO2 is dropping! What do I do?
questions.answer:
**Experience-based guidance:** These notes draw on personal caregiving experience and shared family learning. They are not a clinician-validated emergency protocol or a substitute for the person’s written, individualized emergency plan and hands-on training with the treating team.

**Call for help early:** Call 112 immediately in India for severe or worsening breathing difficulty, ineffective ventilation, suspected blocked or displaced tracheostomy, blue/grey colour, collapse or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for a particular SpO2 reading or try every step first.

**Call and care in parallel:** One person stays with PALS and provides only trained, prescribed support while another calls emergency services and the treating respiratory/ICU team. If alone, call on speakerphone while staying with PALS.

**Immediate checks within your training:** Check external power, visible connections and tubing for disconnection or kinks. Ask about symptoms and report alarms and breathing changes. Suction only when indicated and as prescribed and taught for this person; do not routinely instil saline into the tracheostomy.

**Know when to stop:** If external checks and any prescribed, trained suction do not promptly restore effective breathing, stop repeated attempts and obtain urgent skilled help. If the person worsens, escalate immediately. Do not delay help for nebulization or repeated suction cycles.

**Suction catheter will not pass:** If the suction catheter will not pass, the TT tube may be blocked or displaced. Call 112 and the respiratory/ICU team now. Do not force the catheter, squeeze an Ambu bag harder, or attempt ventilation through a tube whose patency and position are uncertain.

**Who should manage the airway:** TT removal/replacement and cuff interventions require a doctor, respiratory therapist or ICU nurse competent and authorized in emergency tracheostomy care. A ventilator technician can help with equipment, but must have specific clinical training and authorization to perform airway procedures. A caregiver should perform an airway intervention only if specifically trained and authorized in that person’s written emergency plan.

**While help is coming:** Follow the written emergency plan and dispatcher instructions. Bring the airway plan, tube details, prescribed spare equipment and medication list. Report actions already taken. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow resuscitation instructions and the agreed care plan.

[Read the emergency guidance and sources](/emergency-protocol).

questions.question: Power cut at night! BiPAP stopped. What's the emergency plan?
questions.answer:
**Experience-based guidance:** These notes draw on personal caregiving experience and shared family learning. They are not a clinician-validated emergency protocol or a substitute for the person’s written, individualized emergency plan and hands-on training with the treating team.

**During a power interruption:** Check that the prescribed ventilator has switched to its approved backup supply and is working. Respond to alarms and use only the backup method you have been trained to provide.

**If ventilation fails or the person is distressed:** Call 112 immediately in India for severe or worsening breathing difficulty, ineffective ventilation, suspected blocked or displaced tracheostomy, blue/grey colour, collapse or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for a particular SpO2 reading or try every step first. One person stays with PALS and provides only trained, prescribed support while another calls emergency services and the treating respiratory/ICU team. If alone, call on speakerphone while staying with PALS.

**Manual ventilation:** Use it only according to the individual plan and your training. If the suction catheter will not pass, the TT tube may be blocked or displaced. Call 112 and the respiratory/ICU team now. Do not force the catheter, squeeze an Ambu bag harder, or attempt ventilation through a tube whose patency and position are uncertain.

**Prepare before an outage:** Have the equipment provider and electrician verify compatibility, actual load, transfer behaviour, battery condition and tested runtime. No single inverter size or battery duration suits every setup. Arrange transfer early if the backup will not cover the outage.

[Power planning guide](/power-backup-guide) · [Emergency guidance](/emergency-protocol).

questions.question: What is the Ambu bag and how do we use it?
questions.answer:
**What it is:** An Ambu bag is a manual resuscitator that a trained person may use for backup ventilation under a patient-specific plan. It is not a general treatment for discomfort, a low SpO2 reading or a high pulse/BP.

**Learn before an emergency:** Ask the respiratory team to teach the correct interface, connections, technique, assessment of effective ventilation and when to stop. Do not improvise connections to a running ventilator or follow a universal squeeze count from a website.

**Call and care together:** Call 112 immediately in India for severe or worsening breathing difficulty, ineffective ventilation, suspected blocked or displaced tracheostomy, blue/grey colour, collapse or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for a particular SpO2 reading or try every step first. One person stays with PALS and provides only trained, prescribed support while another calls emergency services and the treating respiratory/ICU team. If alone, call on speakerphone while staying with PALS.

**Suspected blocked or displaced TT:** If the suction catheter will not pass, the TT tube may be blocked or displaced. Call 112 and the respiratory/ICU team now. Do not force the catheter, squeeze an Ambu bag harder, or attempt ventilation through a tube whose patency and position are uncertain. TT removal/replacement and cuff interventions require a doctor, respiratory therapist or ICU nurse competent and authorized in emergency tracheostomy care. A ventilator technician can help with equipment, but must have specific clinical training and authorization to perform airway procedures. categories.name: Daily Care & Comfort
categories.description: Bedsores, secretions, constipation, and routine comfort care

questions.question: How do we manage constipation?
questions.answer:
**Constipation is very common in ALS** due to reduced mobility and medications. Here's a proven protocol:

**1. DIETARY CHANGES (First Step):**
• High fiber foods: Papaya, pears, apple, spinach, bottle gourd
• Add flax seed powder to feeds
• Adequate fluid intake

**2. STOOL SOFTENERS:**
• PEG (Movicol/Polyethylene Glycol): 17gm in water daily
• Pruvict 2mg tablet with PEG

**3. IF STILL CONSTIPATED (Day 3):**
• Piclin syrup 10ml OR Cremalax 5-10mg tablet
• Glycerine suppository if needed

**4. LAST RESORT:**
• Glycerine enema (safe)
• Sodium phosphate enema only if absolutely necessary (can cause electrolyte imbalance)

questions.question: How do we prevent and treat bed sores?
questions.answer:
**PREVENTION (Most Important):**
• Position changes every 2-3 hours
• Use air mattress (Romsons Cell Mat or similar)
• Keep skin clean and dry
• Use pillows for proper positioning
• Apply coconut oil on pressure points
• Use Abzorb powder for mild sores

**High-Risk Areas:** Tailbone, heels, back of head, shoulders, elbows

**FOR EXISTING SORES:**
• Stage 1 (Red skin): More position changes, air exposure, coconut oil
• Stage 2-3 (Open wound): Clean with NS and betadine, Cuticell gauze
• Consult doctor if sores are deep or infected
questions.warning: Deep wounds, signs of infection (pus, redness, swelling), bone visible - seek immediate medical help

questions.question: What can help with excess saliva (sialorrhea)?
questions.answer:
**Options for managing excess saliva:**

• **Glycopyrrolate (1-2mg):** Start with small dose (1mg). Watch for side effect - can dry out chest and thicken phlegm.

• **Atropine drops:** Under tongue, helps reduce saliva

• **Botox injections:** Into salivary glands, longer lasting effect

• **Suction:** Keep suction ready for managing excess saliva
questions.warning: Drying medications can thicken mucus in the lungs, making it harder to clear. Balance is key - managing excess saliva is better than completely drying it out.

categories.name: Medications & Supplements
categories.description: Common medications, supplements, and vaccinations for ALS patients

questions.question: What is Riluzole and should my PALS take it?
questions.answer:
**Riluzole (Rilutor/Reluzole)** is the only FDA-approved drug that has been shown to modestly slow ALS progression.

**How it works:** Reduces glutamate toxicity (a neurotransmitter that can damage nerve cells)

**Dosage:** Usually 50mg twice daily

**Side effects:** Some experience dizziness initially (usually improves in 1-2 weeks), nausea, fatigue

**Community experience:** Many take it continuously for years. Those who experienced dizziness often found it resolved. Some stopped due to side effects.

if_then.then: Try reducing to once daily temporarily, then gradually increase

questions.recommendation: Consult your neurologist before making any changes to Riluzole dosage.

questions.question: What other medications might help?
questions.answer:
**Common medications used** (always consult your doctor):

**FOR MUSCLE CRAMPS/SPASTICITY:**
• Baclofen, Tizanidine
• Gabapentin (also helps with pain)

**FOR PSEUDOBULBAR AFFECT (uncontrolled laughing/crying):**
• Nuedexta

**FOR SECRETION MANAGEMENT:**
• Mucinac 600 (thins mucus)
• Glycopyrrolate (reduces saliva - use cautiously)

**FOR GASTRIC ISSUES:**
• Acogut (for acid reflux - works well per community)
• Sompraz IT / Nexpro IT (with itopride for better results)

**FOR INFECTIONS:**
• Antibiotics targeting Pseudomonas (common in trach patients): Levofloxacin, Ofloxacin, Ciprofloxacin
• Always do sputum culture to identify specific bacteria
questions.warning: All prescription medications should only be taken as advised by treating physician.

questions.question: What vaccinations should PALS get?
questions.answer:
**Recommended Vaccinations:**

1. **Influvac Tetra:** Annual flu vaccine - important as flu can be serious for ventilator-dependent patients

2. **Prevnar 13:** Pneumococcal vaccine (13-strain)

3. **Pneumococcal 23:** Another pneumococcal vaccine

**Purpose:** Prevents serious respiratory infections that can be life-threatening for ALS patients.

**Timing:** Discuss with doctor. Usually given when patient is stable, not during active infection.

categories.name: Caregiver Support & Well-being
categories.description: Preventing burnout, managing stress, training staff, and getting support

questions.question: I'm exhausted from caregiving. How do others cope?
questions.answer:
**Caregiver burnout is real and serious.** Here's what has helped others:

**1. BUILD A CARE TEAM:**
• Hire trained nursing staff if possible
• Rotate family members for different shifts
• Train backup caregivers for all critical tasks

**2. TAKE BREAKS:**
• Even 30 minutes of personal time daily helps
• Arrange respite care for longer breaks

**3. CONNECT WITH COMMUNITY:**
• Join support groups (WhatsApp, Facebook)
• Share experiences with others who understand

**4. SEEK HELP WHEN NEEDED:**
• Don't hesitate to see a counselor or psychologist
• Antidepressants may help if feeling overwhelmed
perspectives: You cannot pour from an empty cup
Taking care of yourself IS taking care of your PALS
questions.warning: Persistent depression, anxiety, or inability to cope - seek professional help immediately

questions.question: How do we keep our PALS mentally engaged and positive?
questions.answer:
**Keeping quality of life high:**

• **Involve them in decisions:** About their care, daily routine, family matters

• **Enable communication:** Eye-tracking devices, communication boards, Alexa/voice-controlled devices

• **Maintain connections:** Video calls with family and friends, visits when possible

• **Entertainment:** Audiobooks, movies, music they enjoy

• **Outings:** Even short trips outside (with proper preparation) can boost morale tremendously
perspectives: After 6 years with ALS, we took our PALS outside for the first time in months. The smile on her face made all the preparation worth it.

questions.question: What is the two-person approach for emergencies?
questions.answer:
These notes draw on personal caregiving experience and shared family learning. They are not a clinician-validated emergency protocol or a substitute for the person’s written, individualized emergency plan and hands-on training with the treating team.

**Call and care together:** One person stays with PALS and provides only trained, prescribed support while another calls emergency services and the treating respiratory/ICU team. If alone, call on speakerphone while staying with PALS.

Call 112 immediately in India for severe or worsening breathing difficulty, ineffective ventilation, suspected blocked or displaced tracheostomy, blue/grey colour, collapse or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for a particular SpO2 reading or try every step first.

**Know when to stop:** If external checks and any prescribed, trained suction do not promptly restore effective breathing, stop repeated attempts and obtain urgent skilled help. If the person worsens, escalate immediately. Do not delay help for nebulization or repeated suction cycles.

TT removal/replacement and cuff interventions require a doctor, respiratory therapist or ICU nurse competent and authorized in emergency tracheostomy care. A ventilator technician can help with equipment, but must have specific clinical training and authorization to perform airway procedures. A caregiver should perform an airway intervention only if specifically trained and authorized in that person’s written emergency plan.

key_numbers.spo2_alert: Use individualized targets and symptoms; seek prompt clinical advice for an unexpected fall.
key_numbers.spo2_emergency: Severe distress or ineffective ventilation is an emergency regardless of SpO2; call 112 immediately.

key_principles: Involve PALS in all decisions - they understand their body best
Prevention beats cure - regular nebulization, hydration, position changes prevent emergencies
Use manual ventilation only under the individual emergency plan and your training; never force ventilation through a suspected blocked or displaced tube.
Have backups for EVERYTHING critical - BiPAP, suction, power
Document and learn - every PALS is different
Take care of yourself - caregiver health matters
You are not alone - community is here to support you 24/7
Plan ahead - don't wait for emergencies to arrange equipment
Start interventions early - BiPAP, PEG work better before crisis
Focus on quality of life - many PALS live 5, 8, even 10+ years with good care
